notes: Section 4.4 replaces create-before-destroy-order with create-before-destroy-does-not-force-replacement to avoid a name giveaway. Section 5.1 replaces nonregistry-module-version-argument with module-source-literal to avoid retesting the registry-only version distinction.

cards.statement: A resource attribute reference makes Terraform order the referring resource after its target.
cards.explanation: Terraform infers operation order from resource references, placing the referenced resource first.

cards.statement: The depends_on meta-argument declares an ordering need that resource attributes leave hidden.
cards.explanation: Use depends_on when a resource relies on another resource’s behavior but uses none of its values.

cards.statement: A depends_on on a module call delays just the child output used by the caller.
cards.explanation: A module-level depends_on affects every resource and data source in the child module, not just one output.
cards.misconception: A module dependency applies only to a referenced output.

cards.statement: create_before_destroy forces replacement for a change that supports an in-place update.
cards.explanation: The rule changes the order of a replacement Terraform already needs; it does not turn in-place updates into replacements.
cards.misconception: create_before_destroy converts in-place updates into replacements.

cards.statement: Terraform confines create_before_destroy to the resource declaring the lifecycle rule.
cards.explanation: Terraform propagates create_before_destroy behavior to dependencies of the resource that declares it.
cards.misconception: Upstream resource dependencies never inherit create_before_destroy.

cards.statement: ignore_changes skips a configured attribute when Terraform first creates a resource.
cards.explanation: Terraform still considers ignored attributes when creating a resource; ignore_changes suppresses later update differences.
cards.misconception: ignore_changes omits the named argument during initial creation.

cards.statement: A failed precondition stops Terraform before it acts on the associated resource.
cards.explanation: Terraform evaluates a resource precondition before its action and stops that action if the condition fails.

cards.statement: A custom condition’s error_message requires a fixed string literal.
cards.explanation: Terraform accepts any string-producing expression for error_message, including templates that include evaluated values.
cards.misconception: A custom validation message cannot include evaluated values.

cards.statement: A failed check block reports a warning while Terraform continues its operation.
cards.explanation: A check assertion can report an unmet condition without blocking the plan or apply operation.

cards.statement: Terraform evaluates input variable validation while it builds a plan.
cards.explanation: A variable validation checks supplied values before Terraform finishes the plan and stops an invalid operation.

cards.statement: The sensitive argument omits an ordinary resource argument’s value from state.
cards.explanation: The sensitive argument redacts CLI and HCP Terraform UI output, but Terraform still stores the value in state and plan files.
cards.misconception: Marking a variable sensitive prevents its storage in state.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

cards.statement: An ephemeral input variable can supply a value to a provider block.
cards.explanation: Provider configuration is an allowed ephemeral context, so a runtime credential can avoid persistence in state and plan files.

cards.statement: A root module output can forward a child module’s ephemeral output value.
cards.explanation: Terraform permits ephemeral output blocks in child modules, while root module outputs cannot be ephemeral or expose an ephemeral value.
cards.misconception: Root outputs can pass ephemeral values onward.

cards.statement: An ephemeral block opens its temporary resource when Terraform needs its result.
cards.explanation: Terraform opens an ephemeral resource on demand and closes it after dependent work for that run phase.

cards.statement: A managed resource’s write-only argument persists its input value in Terraform state.
cards.explanation: Terraform passes a write-only value to the provider during a run, then omits that value from state and plan files.
cards.misconception: Write-only resource arguments are retained like ordinary arguments.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

cards.statement: A provider determines which ephemeral resource types Terraform can declare in a configuration.
cards.explanation: Terraform provides the ephemeral block syntax; the provider implements the available temporary resource types.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

cards.statement: The Vault provider can fetch short-lived credentials for use in a Terraform run.
cards.explanation: Terraform can use the Vault provider to retrieve credentials generated by Vault for another provider to use.

source.title: Inject secrets into Terraform using the Vault provider

cards.statement: Provider-specific credential environment variables require matching Terraform variable blocks.
cards.explanation: Providers can read their supported environment variables directly; Terraform variable blocks are for Terraform input values.
cards.misconception: Provider environment variables work through matching Terraform inputs.

cards.statement: An ephemeral input variable can feed an ordinary managed resource argument.
cards.explanation: Ephemeral values work in specific contexts, such as provider configuration and write-only resource arguments, rather than ordinary resource arguments.
cards.misconception: Any resource argument can consume an ephemeral value.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

cards.statement: HashiCorp’s Terraform style guide advises keeping state files out of version control.
cards.explanation: State can contain sensitive values; the style guide says to ignore state files and their backups in version control.

cards.statement: A module source beginning with ./ loads code from a local directory.
cards.explanation: The ./ prefix identifies module source files already present on the local filesystem.

cards.statement: A Git module source can target a subdirectory using // after the repository path.
cards.explanation: The // segment selects a subdirectory inside the downloaded Git package.

cards.statement: A module source from the public Terraform Registry uses a git:: repository address.
cards.explanation: Public registry modules use a namespace/name/provider source address; git:: identifies a direct Git source.
cards.misconception: Public registry modules are addressed like direct Git repositories.

cards.statement: A module block can pass a resource attribute as an input to its child module.
cards.explanation: Module inputs are arguments on the call, and Terraform can evaluate a resource reference as an input value.

cards.statement: A parent module can read a child resource attribute through the child’s local resource address.
cards.explanation: A child module exposes values through output blocks; the parent reads them as module.child.output.
cards.misconception: Child resource addresses are visible directly in the parent.

cards.statement: A root module’s input variable is available as var.name inside a child module.
cards.explanation: Variables are scoped to their module. The parent passes a value through the module call to a variable declared by the child.
cards.misconception: Root input variables automatically enter child module scope.

cards.statement: The version argument constrains which public registry release a module call can install.
cards.explanation: Terraform selects a registry module version that satisfies the call’s version constraint.

cards.statement: A module call can build its source path from an input variable expression.
cards.explanation: A module source must be a literal string; Terraform does not evaluate variable expressions in that argument.
cards.misconception: Module source accepts interpolated runtime values.

cards.statement: A module block’s count creates child instances addressed with numeric indexes.
cards.explanation: The count meta-argument gives each module instance an index, such as module.child[0].

cards.statement: A nested module call starts a separate Terraform run.
cards.explanation: Nested module calls belong to the same configuration tree and are managed as part of one Terraform run.
cards.misconception: Nested child modules run as separate Terraform configurations.

cards.statement: Terraform selects the local backend and stores state on disk by default.
cards.explanation: The local state file stays on the machine running Terraform, so other users do not share it by default.

cards.statement: The local backend’s path setting sets the state filename for non-default CLI workspaces.
cards.explanation: For the local backend, path names the main state file; workspace_dir controls where non-default CLI workspaces store state.
cards.misconception: The path option names state files for every CLI workspace.

cards.statement: The local backend locks state through operating system APIs during writes.
cards.explanation: The local backend uses system APIs to lock its local state file while Terraform performs write-capable operations.

cards.statement: Terraform stops an operation that could write state when acquiring its lock fails.
cards.explanation: Terraform halts the operation rather than continue with an unlocked state write that could conflict with another run.

cards.statement: Terraform supplies state locking regardless of the selected backend’s capabilities.
cards.explanation: Locking depends on the backend; some backends have no locking support.
cards.misconception: Terraform provides locking independently of backend support.

cards.statement: A backend block inside a child module changes where that child stores state.
cards.explanation: A backend is configured for the root configuration. Child module resources share that configuration’s state.
cards.misconception: Each child module can configure its own state backend.

cards.statement: A backend block can use an input variable to choose its storage location.
cards.explanation: Backend configuration cannot reference named values such as input variables; supply varying settings during initialization.
cards.misconception: Backend settings evaluate input variables like resource arguments.

cards.statement: terraform init can complete a partial backend configuration using an external settings file.
cards.explanation: The file supplies backend arguments omitted from the root configuration during initialization.

cards.statement: Terraform offers to migrate existing state after a backend configuration change.
cards.explanation: Reinitialization after a backend change can copy the existing state into the new backend.

cards.statement: A non-local backend writes a local state file after each successful Terraform operation.
cards.explanation: Terraform normally handles state from non-local backends in memory and writes it locally only after an unrecoverable backend write failure.
cards.misconception: Remote state is routinely copied to a local state file.
